chunks.content:
Running every task about four times is the same as running the whole benchmark about four
times, so each configuration has roughly four benchmark scores. The first score grades each task
on its first rollout, the second score grades each task on its second rollout, and so on (we order a
task’s rollouts by start time). Call these scores s1, . . . , sR. If a configuration is stable, its scores
land close together; if it is noisy, they spread out. We report that spread as a 95% confidence
interval, pass@1 ± 1.96 SE, where the standard error of the mean is SE = std(s1, . . . , sR)/

R. This
convention follows Terminal-Bench [Merrill et al., 2026]; we release the per-run scores and the code
that computes them. These intervals are the whiskers in Figure 1, and they caution against reading
the leaderboard as a strict ranking: GPT-5.5 sits clearly apart at the top (70.0%, [67.2, 72.9]), while
mid-table neighbors such as GPT-5.4 (55.5%, [53.4, 57.7]) and Claude Opus 4.7 (54.2%, [49.5, 58.9])
have overlapping intervals and so are not statistically separated.

This interval captures only one source of noise: how much the score moves when we rerun the
same 113 tasks. It misses a second source: the benchmark is just one particular set of 113 tasks,
and a different but equally reasonable set could have given a different score. The interval also
has a small-sample weakness. With only about four runs, a configuration whose runs happen
to land close together looks very precise even when its true uncertainty is large [Wang, 2025,
Terminal-Bench contributors, 2026]. Methods that also account for which tasks were chosen give
wider intervals [Madaan et al., 2024]. One option is a cluster bootstrap: repeatedly build a new
113-task benchmark by drawing tasks at random (with replacement) from our 113 tasks, keeping
each drawn task’s rollouts together, rescore each time, and read the spread of those scores; this shows
how much the result depends on the particular tasks. Even a Wilson interval, a standard confidence
interval for a success rate computed over all attempts pooled together, is wider here: [65.6, 74.1] for
GPT-5.5, against [67.2, 72.9] run-to-run. We report the run-to-run interval for comparability with
existing leaderboards.
